text:
I need an email to win back customers who cancelled. I own a home cleaning company with 18 cleaners.

What's true:
- We have 212 regular customers. 64 cancelled in the last year. In exit surveys, the most common reason was price, then a different cleaner showing up each time.
- An every-other-week cleaning for a 3-bedroom house costs $165 with us. The app services in our area charge about $140.
- Our cleaners are employees, not contractors. We pay $21 an hour and carry insurance on every visit.
- Last year 7 of our 18 cleaners left, so about 4 in 10 customers had their regular cleaner change at least once.
- We now give each customer a regular cleaner and a named backup.
- Returning customers get their first cleaning for $99.

I want the email to promise that you'll get the same cleaner every single time. Keep it to about 150 words.

I can write this, but the "same cleaner every single time" promise is a problem.

**The promise doesn't match what you can deliver.** You now give each customer a regular cleaner and a named backup. That means some visits will be the backup. Last year 7 of your 18 cleaners left. If a customer's regular cleaner leaves next year, "every single time" is broken in writing. These are people who already left partly because the cleaner kept changing, so a promise that fails is worse than none. Here's what your facts do support: "You'll have your own regular cleaner. If they're ever out, it's one named backup you already know, never a stranger." That still answers their complaint directly. Do you want that version, or do you have something that would back the stronger promise?

Some questions that would change the email:

1. **Has anything changed with cleaner turnover?** Raises, better schedules, or fewer people leaving this year all count. The reader will think "you said that before," and this is the best answer to it.
2. **What happens after the $99 cleaning?** Does it go back to $165? Is there a deadline or any commitment? Customers will check this before they book.
3. **What does the extra $25 buy compared with the apps?** I can use employees at $21 an hour and insurance on every visit. Do you know whether the app services' cleaners are uninsured contractors? I won't claim it unless you can confirm it.
4. **Can you name their old cleaner, or their new one?** "Maria would be your regular cleaner" is much stronger than a general promise, if your mailing tool can fill in names.
5. **Who signs it, and how do they book?** A reply, a link, or a phone number?
6. **Is there anything else they'd know or find out?** For example, a price increase coming, or a cleaner they liked who has since left.

If you'd rather skip these, I'll write it now from the facts you gave, using the regular-plus-backup promise.

Yes, use the regular cleaner plus named backup version, but make it as strong as you can without saying anything false. I can't promise every single time because of sick days and holidays.

1. Yes. Since we started giving each customer a regular cleaner in July, only 1 of our 18 cleaners has left.
2. It goes back to our regular price. The $99 offer ends December 31. There's no contract, and they can cancel any time.
3. Yes, the app services here mostly use contractors who carry no insurance on the visit.
4. I don't know if our mailing tool can fill in names.
5. Lisa Grant, owner, Brightway Home Cleaning. They book by replying to the email or calling 555-0164.
6. I can't match $140 a visit, so please don't suggest that we will.

I've written the email at about 150 words with the regular-plus-backup promise.

<final_document>
Subject: A regular cleaner you know, and $99 to come back

Hi,

When customers cancelled last year, the reasons we heard most were price and too many different cleaners at the door. The second one was on us: 7 of our 18 cleaners left, and about 4 in 10 customers saw their cleaner change.

Since July, every customer has their own regular cleaner, plus one named backup for sick days and holidays. You'll always know who's coming. Since then, only 1 of our 18 cleaners has left.

We charge $165 every other week for a 3-bedroom home, and the apps charge about $140. The difference pays for cleaners who are our employees, earn $21 an hour and are insured on every visit. Most app cleaners here are contractors with no insurance on the visit.

Come back and your first cleaning is $99, then our regular price. There's no contract, and you can cancel any time. The offer ends December 31.

Reply to this email or call 555-0164 to book.

Lisa Grant
Owner, Brightway Home Cleaning
</final_document>

- **Turnover:** The email admits last year's turnover before giving the July numbers. These customers lived through it. Owning it makes "only 1 of 18 since July" believable instead of sounding like marketing.
- **Price:** Your $165 and the apps' $140 each appear once, next to what the extra $25 pays for. Nothing suggests you'll match their price.
- **"You'll always know who's coming":** This is the strongest true line about cleaners, and it holds even on backup days. Cut it if your backup assignments sometimes change.
- **Sending:** Before it goes out, check whether $165 is the right price for these customers. The email quotes the 3-bedroom rate, so customers with other home sizes may need a different version. Also, if your mailing tool can fill in each customer's cleaner and backup by name, use that. It's the most convincing thing you could add.
